one_line_idea: Any fixed-feature-space distance metric for generative image evaluation is structurally gameable, and an adversarial-sensitivity audit should accompany every reported score.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Generative image quality is summarized by distances between feature distributions computed in a fixed embedding space, and such scores steer model development.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For any fixed feature extractor there exist generator modifications that improve the score while degrading human-judged quality, and modern training pipelines partially find such directions implicitly, so scores drift from human judgment as optimization pressure increases.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Directly optimizing a generator or a post-hoc filter against the metric will yield samples with better scores and flat-or-worse human preference, and the exploit direction will transfer partially across generators.
why_important: The field's automatic quality numbers are optimization targets; unaudited gameability means reported progress can decouple from perceptual quality without anyone noticing.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Metric gaming is known in principle; a standardized adversarial-sensitivity audit protocol with transferability measurements across current metrics and feature spaces may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Attach a small learnable post-processing module to a fixed generator, optimize it against the metric only, and run a human preference study comparing pre and post samples.
main_risk: Human studies are costly, and small perceptual degradations may need large rater pools to detect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Feature-distance scores are treated as reliable proxies for perceptual quality across the current operating range.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A frozen feature space defines a fixed blind-spot structure, and sustained optimization pressure finds blind spots regardless of which extractor is chosen.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Optimize sample selection, not generation, against the metric from a fixed pool and check whether the score improves while a small human panel sees no improvement; days.

one_line_idea: Averaging accuracy uniformly over corruption types assumes all corruptions are equally likely, and deployment-weighted robustness scores flip model rankings.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Corruption-robustness benchmarks report an unweighted mean over a fixed menu of corruption types and severities.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Real deployment corruption distributions are heavily non-uniform and context-dependent, and under plausible deployment weightings the ranking of robust models changes, so the unweighted mean is not decision-relevant for any actual deployment.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Constructing several empirically motivated corruption-frequency profiles, for example from vehicle, mobile, and webcam contexts, and re-scoring public checkpoints will produce different winners across profiles and versus the unweighted mean.
why_important: Robustness leaderboards influence augmentation research and model choice; a weighting-sensitive ranking means the single number answers a question nobody asked.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Weighting critiques are occasionally voiced; delivering measured deployment corruption profiles plus a re-ranking analysis may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate corruption-type frequencies from public in-the-wild image collections per context, re-weight existing per-corruption scores of many checkpoints, and quantify ranking changes.
main_risk: Estimating corruption frequencies from found data involves its own detection errors and selection biases.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The unweighted corruption mean is treated as a neutral, general-purpose robustness summary.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Uniform weighting is itself a strong assumption, and neutrality between corruption types is not neutrality between deployments.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Reweight published per-corruption results of public models under three hand-specified plausible profiles and check for rank flips; hours, no inference.

one_line_idea: Zero-shot retrieval recall correlates poorly with the end-task utility of embeddings inside retrieval-augmented multimodal pipelines.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Embedding models are ranked by recall-at-k on retrieval benchmarks and then adopted inside retrieval-augmented generation systems whose end metric is answer quality.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Beyond a threshold, recall gains stop translating into end-task gains because errors shift to failure modes recall does not measure, such as retrieving redundant or subtly misleading neighbors, so embedding leaderboards misorder models for pipeline use.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Holding the generator fixed and swapping embedding models across a wide recall range will show a weak, plateauing relation between benchmark recall and end-task answer quality, with rank inversions among the top embedding models.
why_important: Embedding choice is one of the few components teams select purely by leaderboard; a weak proxy link means those selections are close to arbitrary at the top.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Proxy-metric concerns exist in text retrieval; a systematic proxy-validity study for multimodal retrieval-augmented pipelines may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix one multimodal question-answering pipeline, swap eight embedding models of varying benchmark recall, and measure end-task quality with matched retrieval depth.
main_risk: End-task quality depends on generator-retriever interaction effects that one fixed generator may not represent.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Higher retrieval recall is assumed to yield better retrieval-augmented system performance more or less monotonically.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Recall counts topical hits while the pipeline needs evidence quality, and the two diverge exactly where modern embeddings compete.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three embedding models spanning the leaderboard, one small question set, one fixed generator; compare end-task scores in days.

one_line_idea: Model-based image-caption metrics are circular: they systematically favor captions stylistically similar to the judge's own training distribution, penalizing accurate but differently phrased descriptions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Caption quality is increasingly scored by learned metrics built on the same families of image-text models being evaluated.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Learned caption metrics reward distributional similarity to web alt-text style over factual visual accuracy, so systems trained toward these metrics converge on judge-pleasing phrasing, and metric gains overstate accuracy gains.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Constructing caption pairs matched for human-rated accuracy but differing in style will show learned metrics preferring judge-style captions at a high rate, and this preference will grow with judge-caption model family overlap.
why_important: Captioning and dense description research is steering toward learned judges; unmeasured circularity converts the research objective into imitation of the judge.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Judge-bias concerns are active in language evaluation; a controlled style-versus-accuracy factorial study for image captioning metrics may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Create a factorial caption set crossing accuracy level with style, collect human accuracy ratings, and measure each learned metric's sensitivity to style at fixed accuracy.
main_risk: Disentangling style from accuracy in natural captions is delicate and needs careful stimulus construction.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Learned caption metrics are assumed to approximate human accuracy judgments better than n-gram metrics across the board.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The judge's notion of caption quality was learned from the same skewed alt-text distribution the captioners imitate, closing a stylistic loop that excludes accuracy.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Rewrite 100 human-verified captions into a different accurate style and check the learned-metric score drop; one day including light human verification.

one_line_idea: AUROC-based out-of-distribution detection rankings do not survive at deployment-relevant operating points, and FPR-at-high-TPR reorders published methods.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Out-of-distribution detection is summarized by threshold-free area metrics, while deployments operate at a single stringent threshold.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Method rankings by area metrics and by false-positive rate at stringent true-positive requirements disagree frequently enough that leaderboard order is uninformative for deployment, because area metrics reward performance in operationally irrelevant regions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-scoring a broad set of reproduced detection methods at fixed stringent operating points will show frequent pairwise rank flips versus area-metric order, concentrated among methods with crossing receiver curves.
why_important: Practitioners pick detectors from leaderboards; if the summary metric ignores the operating regime, the pick is uncorrelated with deployment value.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Operating-point critiques are generic in classification; a quantified rank-instability audit across the modern detection method zoo may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reproduce ten detection methods on standard pairs, compute area metrics and stringent-threshold metrics, and report the pairwise flip rate with bootstrap uncertainty.
main_risk: Reproduction quality varies across methods, and implementation gaps could be mistaken for metric disagreement.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Higher area-under-curve is read as a better detector overall, including at strict thresholds.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Receiver curves of competing methods cross, and the area integrates over regions that deployments never visit.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two methods with public score files, compute both metric types, exhibit one flip; an hour.

one_line_idea: Multi-task benchmark suite rankings are unstable under reasonable task reweighting, so suite-level leaderboards encode arbitrary editorial weight choices.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Foundation models are compared by averaging scores across task collections whose composition and implicit weighting were set by benchmark authors.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For current model pools, the leaderboard order changes under many defensible reweightings, such as equalizing task families, difficulty, or deployment relevance, so suite rank is an artifact of composition choices rather than a robust capability ordering.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Computing the ranking distribution over a large space of defensible weightings will show that only extreme-gap model pairs have stable order, while adjacent leaderboard positions flip under a substantial fraction of weightings.
why_important: Suite leaderboards are the primary public evidence in model release claims; weight-instability quantifies how much of that evidence is editorial.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Weighting sensitivity is known in social-choice terms; applying a formal ranking-stability analysis with published instability certificates for vision suites may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take per-task public scores for one suite, sample defensible weightings under stated constraints, and publish per-pair order-stability probabilities.
main_risk: Defining the space of defensible weightings is contestable, so results must be shown robust to the definition.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The suite average is treated as a canonical scalar capability measure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averaging incommensurable task scores requires a weighting choice, and no choice is neutral once models specialize differently.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Per-task scores of five models, one thousand random simplex weightings, count rank flips; an hour on a laptop.

one_line_idea: Repeated-sampling metrics for multimodal generation conflate output diversity with capability, crediting models for stochastic variety rather than reliability.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Best-of-k style metrics reward a model if any of several sampled outputs succeeds, and are increasingly used for multimodal reasoning and generation tasks.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Best-of-k rankings can be driven by sampling temperature and output diversity rather than by the probability of being correct on demand, so they misorder models for single-shot deployment and invert under reliability metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping decoding temperature will move best-of-k scores substantially at fixed model weights, and model rankings under best-of-k will differ from rankings under first-sample accuracy on the same tasks.
why_important: Deployments mostly consume one sample; a leaderboard that rewards lottery-ticket diversity selects models misaligned with use.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The diversity-reliability distinction is discussed for code models; a controlled decomposition for multimodal tasks with temperature-sweep evidence may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate several models at multiple temperatures under best-of-k and first-sample metrics on one multimodal task, and quantify how much best-of-k rank is temperature-explainable.
main_risk: Some applications genuinely use best-of-k with verifiers, for which the metric is appropriate, so scope must be stated carefully.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Best-of-k improvements are read as capability improvements.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The metric measures the union of k draws, which grows with output entropy independently of per-draw correctness.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, three temperatures, best-of-8 versus first-sample on a small task set; an evening.

one_line_idea: Micro-averaged accuracy hides that foundation-model progress is concentrated on frequent classes, and macro-averaged evaluation shows much flatter progress curves.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard accuracy weights items equally, which under skewed class distributions weights classes by frequency, and progress claims are made on this micro average.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Re-scoring historical and current checkpoints with macro-averaged per-class accuracy will show that a disproportionate share of claimed multi-year progress comes from head classes, with tail-class progress substantially slower, changing the shape of the field's progress narrative.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The macro-accuracy progress curve across model generations will be flatter than the micro curve, and the head-tail progress gap will widen for web-pretrained models relative to supervised-era models.
why_important: If progress is frequency-concentrated, capability claims overstate readiness for tail-heavy applications, which are common in specialized domains.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Long-tail evaluation exists as a subfield; applying the macro lens retrospectively to the foundation-model progress narrative across generations may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a chronological pool of public checkpoints with micro and macro metrics on one large benchmark and compare progress-curve slopes.
main_risk: Macro metrics are noisy on rare classes, requiring uncertainty-aware curve comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Benchmark progress curves are read as broadly distributed capability growth.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Web pretraining data follows heavy-tailed frequency distributions, focusing learning where the metric already concentrates its weight.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Micro and macro scores for five checkpoints spanning several years on one benchmark; hours with cached predictions.

one_line_idea: Uncontrolled prompt-engineering budgets act as hidden compute in zero-shot comparisons, and equalizing prompt-search effort shrinks or reverses claimed model gaps.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Published zero-shot numbers use prompt sets refined to unknown degrees per model, with the search effort undocumented.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The prompt-search budget is a performance-relevant hidden variable of the same order as model differences, and gaps between models change materially when prompt optimization compute is explicitly equalized.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Running a fixed-budget automated prompt search per model from a common starting set will change reported gaps, in some pairs reversing which model looks better relative to using each model's community-tuned prompts.
why_important: Cross-model zero-shot comparisons underlie adoption claims, and an unequalized tuning budget makes them comparisons of community attention rather than of models.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prompt sensitivity is well known; formalizing prompt search as accounted compute with budget-equalized comparison protocols may be new for vision-language evaluation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define a prompt-search algorithm and budget, apply it identically to several models on two benchmarks, and compare budget-equalized gaps against community-prompt gaps.
main_risk: Search algorithm choice may favor certain models, requiring several search strategies to show robustness.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reported zero-shot gaps are treated as intrinsic model differences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Popular models accumulate years of community prompt tuning that newer or less popular models never received.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fixed random-search over prompts with an identical trial count for two models on one benchmark; a day.

one_line_idea: Linear-probe evaluation encodes a linearity assumption about representation quality, and shallow nonlinear probes rerank vision backbones, undermining probe-based pretraining conclusions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Representation quality of pretrained backbones is standardly compared by accuracy of linear classifiers on frozen features.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Backbones differ in how linearly accessible their information is, not only in how much information they encode, so linear-probe rankings conflate the two and small nonlinear probes will reorder backbones by recovering nonlinearly-encoded information.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparing linear probes against capacity-controlled two-layer probes across a pool of backbones will produce reproducible rank changes on some tasks, with disagreement concentrated in backbones trained with objectives that do not encourage linear separability.
why_important: Years of pretraining-method conclusions rest on linear probing; if rankings are probe-dependent, some of those conclusions are protocol artifacts.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Probe-choice sensitivity has been raised in interpretability contexts; a systematic backbone-reranking study framed against the pretraining-evaluation canon may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate ten backbones with linear and matched-budget nonlinear probes on five downstream tasks and quantify rank agreement per task.
main_risk: Nonlinear probes introduce optimization variance, requiring repeated runs to separate signal from probe-training noise.
community_default_belief: [KNOWN FACT] Linear-probe accuracy is the conventional standard for frozen-representation quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Linear accessibility is an objective-dependent property, and objectives differ precisely in this respect across pretraining paradigms.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three backbones, one task, linear versus two-layer probe with equal parameter budget, three seeds; a day.

one_line_idea: Few-shot evaluation variance across support-set draws exceeds the model gaps typically reported, making single-draw few-shot comparisons close to meaningless.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Few-shot results are often reported from one or a few support-set draws, while the draw determines which exemplars define each class.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The across-draw standard deviation of few-shot accuracy for foundation models is comparable to or larger than typical between-model gaps, so many published few-shot orderings would not replicate under redrawn supports.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring the full across-draw distribution for several models will show overlapping distributions for model pairs whose reported point estimates differ by amounts commonly treated as decisive.
why_important: Few-shot capability is a headline foundation-model claim; if the evaluation noise floor swallows the effects, the claims need distributional reporting to mean anything.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Episode variance is acknowledged in the meta-learning literature; quantifying it against the actual reporting practices of the foundation-model era may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several checkpoints and benchmarks, run two hundred support draws per configuration, and compare across-draw dispersion with published-style single-draw gaps.
main_risk: Compute grows with draws times models times tasks, requiring efficient evaluation via cached embeddings.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reported few-shot gaps are treated as stable model properties.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With very few support examples, the estimator variance is dominated by exemplar selection, a term the point estimate hides entirely.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model pair, one task, fifty support draws from cached features; distribution overlap plot in hours.

one_line_idea: Frozen-backbone comparisons are confounded by head architecture and head-training recipes, and standardizing heads changes which backbone wins.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Papers comparing pretrained backbones attach task heads whose architecture, regularization, and schedule vary across works and are tuned per backbone to unknown degrees.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Head-recipe variation contributes score variance comparable to backbone differences on several downstream tasks, so backbone rankings are partially head artifacts and change under standardized or budget-equalized head tuning.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A factorial study crossing backbones with head recipes will show significant backbone-head interaction terms and at least some ranking changes between per-backbone-tuned and standardized-head protocols.
why_important: Backbone selection guides infrastructure investment; recipe-confounded rankings misdirect that investment.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Recipe confounding is folklore; a formal factorial decomposition with interaction quantification across modern backbones may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Cross five backbones with four head recipes on three tasks, decompose variance, and compare rankings under both tuning protocols.
main_risk: The full factorial is compute-heavy, though frozen features make each cell cheap.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Downstream scores with a reasonable head are read as measurements of backbone quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The head is where all task adaptation happens in frozen protocols, so its recipe is not a detail but half the system.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two backbones, two head recipes, one task, four cells; check for a crossing interaction in a day.

one_line_idea: Silent normalization-statistics adaptation at test time is inconsistently applied across robustness studies, contaminating a fraction of reported robustness gains.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Some evaluation codebases update or adapt normalization statistics on the test distribution, an intervention known to improve corruption scores, while others do not, and papers rarely state which behavior applies.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A nontrivial share of cross-paper robustness differences is explained by unreported normalization-adaptation behavior in the harnesses used, rather than by the claimed methods.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Auditing popular evaluation harnesses and re-running key comparisons with adaptation explicitly switched on and off will reveal cases where the reported method effect shrinks materially once behavior is equalized.
why_important: Robustness literature synthesizes results across papers; a hidden binary switch of this magnitude corrupts meta-conclusions about which methods work.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Normalization adaptation is itself a published technique; the audit claim that it acts as an unreported confounder across the robustness literature may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Inventory the adaptation behavior of widely used harnesses, select several published comparisons, and reproduce them under both settings to quantify the confound.
main_risk: Identifying which harness produced which published number requires archaeology that may be inconclusive for some papers.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reported robustness gains are attributed to the proposed methods, with the harness assumed neutral.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Harness defaults differ on an intervention worth several accuracy points under corruption, and defaults are exactly what nobody reports.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, one corruption benchmark, one harness run with adaptation toggled; two numbers in hours.

one_line_idea: Image decoding and interpolation library differences alone shift benchmark scores enough to matter, making bit-level evaluation reproducibility a fiction across the field.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Different image-decoding libraries and versions produce numerically different pixel values from the same compressed files, and evaluation stacks differ in these dependencies.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Library-level pixel differences propagate to measurable score differences for modern high-accuracy models at benchmark scale, exceeding the tolerance implicitly assumed when comparing published numbers to a tenth of a point.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating fixed checkpoints on the same benchmark across several decoding and resizing library stacks will produce score spreads that overlap the granularity of typical cross-paper comparisons.
why_important: The field compares models at decimal precision that the software substrate cannot support, which inflates false discovery in leaderboard terms.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual anecdotes about library effects circulate; a systematic multi-stack quantification with recommended reporting tolerances may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build four evaluation stacks differing only in decode and resize libraries, run five checkpoints on two benchmarks, and report per-model score spreads.
main_risk: The measured spread may be small for robust models, making the result an all-clear rather than an alarm, which is still publishable as a negative result but less impactful.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Scores from different papers on the same benchmark are assumed comparable at sub-point granularity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The input bytes to the model are not standardized by the benchmark, only the compressed files are, and decompression is not a deterministic contract across libraries.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One checkpoint, one benchmark, two decode libraries; difference of two numbers in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Single-resolution evaluation systematically biases cross-model comparisons because models are trained at different native resolutions, and resolution-sweep reporting changes conclusions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmarks are evaluated at a fixed input resolution, while public models are trained and tuned at heterogeneous native resolutions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The fixed evaluation resolution advantages models whose training matched it, and per-model best-resolution or resolution-sweep evaluation changes gaps and some rankings, meaning part of reported model differences is resolution mismatch.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping evaluation resolution per model and comparing peak-versus-fixed-resolution scores will show heterogeneous shifts across models and at least occasional ranking changes relative to the fixed-resolution protocol.
why_important: Resolution is a controllable evaluation setting, and pretending it is neutral converts a tunable preprocessing choice into a hidden handicap system.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Resolution sensitivity of individual models is documented; elevating resolution-sweeps to a fairness requirement with quantified ranking impact may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a model pool across a resolution grid on one benchmark, and compare fixed-resolution rankings with per-model-peak rankings.
main_risk: Allowing per-model best resolution could be criticized as overfitting the evaluation; both protocols must be reported with clear semantics.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Evaluating all models at the same resolution is assumed to be the fair protocol.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Sameness of input resolution is not sameness of operating condition when models were built for different resolutions.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two models with different native resolutions, three evaluation resolutions, one benchmark; six numbers in hours.

one_line_idea: Zero-shot classification rankings are unstable under synonym substitution of class names, revealing that benchmark-specific wording quietly advantages some models.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Zero-shot classifiers are constructed from benchmark-provided class name strings, and different models were pretrained on different text distributions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model rankings change materially when class names are replaced by valid synonyms or descriptions, because each model's text encoder has idiosyncratic affinities to specific wordings, so benchmark wording is an unacknowledged model-dependent advantage.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating a model pool under multiple linguistically valid class-naming schemes will show rank instability well above bootstrap noise, and no single model will dominate across naming schemes.
why_important: Wording sensitivity means zero-shot leaderboards partly measure lexical luck, and robust deployment requires wording-stability reporting.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Class-name sensitivity is known anecdotally; a rank-stability analysis across systematic naming schemes as an evaluation-validity claim may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct four naming schemes for one benchmark with lexicographer validation, evaluate a model pool per scheme, and quantify rank stability.
main_risk: Synonyms can subtly change category semantics, so naming schemes need human validation to remain answer-preserving.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Benchmark class names are treated as neutral task definitions rather than model-favoring inputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A class name is a probe into each text encoder's lexical geometry, and the probes were chosen without considering any model, making their favorability arbitrary.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, two naming schemes, three models; check rank stability in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Inconsistent, often unreported use of test-time augmentation across published results contaminates cross-paper comparisons by an amount comparable to claimed method gains.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Test-time augmentation such as multi-crop or flipping improves scores and is applied inconsistently and sometimes silently across published evaluations.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A meaningful fraction of cross-paper score differences on standard benchmarks is attributable to undisclosed test-time augmentation settings rather than modeling contributions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Reproducing a set of published comparisons under explicitly matched augmentation settings will shrink several claimed gaps, and an audit of public evaluation code will find undisclosed augmentation in a nontrivial share of repositories.
why_important: Meta-analyses and surveys aggregate published numbers assuming protocol comparability; a hidden augmentation switch breaks that assumption quietly.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Test-time augmentation is well known as a technique; treating its silent usage as a measurable literature-level confounder with a code-audit methodology may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Audit twenty public evaluation repositories for augmentation behavior, and re-run five cross-paper comparisons under matched settings to quantify gap changes.
main_risk: Repository archaeology may misattribute behavior when code diverged from what produced published numbers.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Published benchmark numbers are assumed to share a common no-augmentation or declared-augmentation convention.
why_it_might_be_wrong: There is no enforcement mechanism, and the incentive gradient points toward quietly using whatever raises the number.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, one benchmark, evaluation with and without standard test-time augmentation; two numbers in hours to size the confound.

one_line_idea: Random-seed variance in fine-tuning is large enough that many claimed state-of-the-art improvements at foundation scale are single-seed lottery wins.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Fine-tuning results are typically reported from one or very few seeds, and seed variance is rarely quantified at foundation scale because runs are expensive.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Across-seed standard deviation of downstream fine-tuning scores for large vision backbones is comparable to typical claimed improvements, so a material fraction of published gains would not replicate under seed resampling.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Running ten seeds for representative fine-tuning setups will yield score distributions whose spread overlaps typical claimed deltas, and reproducing a few published comparisons with multiple seeds will de-significate some of them.
why_important: Publication decisions and method adoption hinge on deltas that may sit inside the seed-noise band nobody measures.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Seed variance is documented for smaller models and language tasks; a quantified variance atlas for modern vision fine-tuning regimes may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select five common fine-tuning configurations, run ten seeds each, publish the variance atlas, and re-test three published deltas against it.
main_risk: Compute cost is the binding constraint, though parameter-efficient fine-tuning variants make multi-seed studies affordable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A reported fine-tuning improvement is assumed reproducible under retraining.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Optimization noise compounds with data-order and augmentation randomness, and the field's effect sizes have shrunk faster than its variance discipline improved.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One configuration, five seeds with parameter-efficient tuning, compare spread to a chosen published delta; days on modest hardware.

one_line_idea: Attention maps of vision transformers fail causal faithfulness tests: regions highlighted as evidence are often not the regions whose removal changes the prediction.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Attention visualizations are widely presented as explanations of what vision transformers look at, in papers and in deployed decision-support tools.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Across modern vision transformer checkpoints, attention-derived saliency has low agreement with counterfactual importance measured by systematic occlusion or feature deletion, so attention maps are decorative rather than explanatory.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring the overlap between attention-ranked regions and deletion-ranked regions across many images and checkpoints will show weak correlation, and deletion of low-attention regions will frequently change predictions.

community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Attention weights are treated as a usable window into model reasoning for vision transformers.

one_line_idea: Reported advantages of self-supervised pretraining over supervised pretraining shrink or vanish on several downstream tasks once augmentation pipelines and compute are strictly equalized.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Self-supervised and supervised pretraining comparisons typically involve different augmentation recipes, training lengths, and tuning effort inherited from each method's development history.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A strictly matched comparison, equalizing augmentations, compute, and tuning budget, will show that part of the claimed self-supervised advantage on downstream transfer is recipe and budget artifact rather than objective superiority.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Under matched conditions, the gap between paradigms will shrink on a majority of transfer tasks relative to gaps implied by comparing published numbers, with some tasks showing no significant difference.
why_important: Pretraining-paradigm beliefs steer enormous compute investments; recipe-confounded evidence misallocates those investments.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Controlled comparisons exist at smaller scale from earlier eras; a rigorous matched-budget re-examination in the current architecture and data regime may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain paired models under both paradigms with identical augmentations, data, compute, and tuning protocol at a mid scale, and evaluate on a standard transfer suite.
main_risk: Equalizing recipes may handicap one paradigm if its performance genuinely depends on paradigm-specific augmentations, making neutrality contestable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Self-supervised pretraining is widely believed to yield more transferable features than supervised pretraining at comparable scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The comparison was never run clean, and each paradigm's numbers embed years of asymmetric tuning attention.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Small-scale paired pretraining with matched recipes on one dataset, evaluated on three transfer tasks; feasible within days of GPU time.

one_line_idea: Scaling up vision models does not improve calibration under distribution shift beyond what improved accuracy mechanically implies: a negative result about scale as an uncertainty cure.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Larger models tend to be more accurate, and calibration metrics correlate with accuracy, leading to claims that scale improves reliability.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] After conditioning on shifted-accuracy, model scale contributes no additional improvement to shifted calibration or selective-prediction quality, so scale buys correctness but not self-knowledge.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across model families spanning orders of magnitude in parameters, regressing shifted calibration on scale with accuracy controls will show a near-zero scale coefficient.
why_important: If reliability does not come free with scale, safety-critical users cannot substitute bigger checkpoints for uncertainty engineering.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Scale-and-calibration observations exist with mixed conclusions; a careful accuracy-controlled analysis across modern vision families under shift may be unresolved.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate checkpoints across scales within several families on shifted benchmarks, compute calibration and selective metrics, and fit accuracy-controlled scale regressions.
main_risk: Within-family scale ladders confound scale with training data and schedule details, requiring family fixed-effects.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Bigger foundation models are assumed to be more reliably calibrated, especially under shift.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Calibration under shift depends on how confidence deforms off-distribution, a property plausibly set by objective and data, not by parameter count.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One family's public scale ladder, one shifted benchmark, calibration versus scale plot with accuracy control; a day from cached logits.

one_line_idea: Sophisticated data-curation pipelines for vision pretraining add little beyond simple deduplication plus basic quality filtering: a controlled negative result on curation complexity.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Elaborate curation pipelines with learned filters and multi-stage scoring are credited with large pretraining gains, but ablations against strong simple baselines are rare and inconsistent.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under matched token and compute budgets, a pipeline of exact plus near-duplicate removal and rudimentary resolution and caption-length filtering captures most of the downstream benefit attributed to complex curation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Pretraining matched models on complexly curated versus simply curated versions of the same raw pool will show downstream differences much smaller than the gains claimed for curation in aggregate comparisons.
why_important: Curation pipelines are becoming proprietary moats and compute sinks; knowing the simple baseline's share of the benefit redirects effort honestly.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Curation papers ablate their own components; an adversarially strong simple baseline defended with matched budgets across multiple downstream suites may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: From one raw web pool, build simple and complex curated subsets at equal size, pretrain matched models on each, and evaluate on a broad transfer suite.
main_risk: Results may be scale-dependent, with curation mattering more at scales the experiment cannot afford.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Advanced learned curation is believed to be a major driver of modern vision pretraining quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Most of the harm in raw web data may come from duplicates and degenerate items that trivial filters already catch.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Mid-scale paired pretraining runs on simply versus complexly curated data from one public pool; days to a week of GPU time.

one_line_idea: Claimed emergent visual abilities in multimodal models are largely artifacts of discontinuous metrics, and smooth scoring reveals smooth scaling: a metric-artifact negative result.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Emergence claims rest on task scores jumping from near-zero to substantial at some scale, with the scores usually being all-or-nothing per item.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For visual tasks claimed as emergent, replacing discontinuous exact-match metrics with graded partial-credit metrics will show smooth capability growth across scale, relocating emergence from the model to the metric.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-scoring scale-ladder outputs on emergence-cited visual tasks with graded metrics will materially reduce or eliminate the discontinuities visible under exact-match scoring.
why_important: Emergence narratives shape safety debates and investment theses; if the phenomenon is a scoring artifact for vision tasks, those narratives need revision.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The metric-artifact account of emergence has been argued for language tasks; a systematic replication across multimodal visual capabilities may be incomplete.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect outputs of one model family across scales on tasks with claimed visual emergence, score under exact-match and graded metrics, and compare scaling-curve shapes.
main_risk: Designing graded metrics that are not arbitrarily lenient requires care, or the smoothness is built in by construction.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Emergent multimodal abilities are widely treated as real threshold phenomena of scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Exact-match scoring maps gradual improvements in output distributions to step functions whenever partial correctness earns zero.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One family, one claimed-emergent visual task, two scoring rules across available scales; hours if outputs are cached.

one_line_idea: Chain-of-thought prompting yields no genuine gain on visual reasoning benchmarks once answer-format effects and extra-token compute are controlled: a null result behind a popular technique.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Chain-of-thought prompting is reported to improve multimodal benchmark scores and is widely adopted, with comparisons usually made against terse-answer baselines under different output formats.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The measured gains on visual reasoning tasks are substantially explained by answer-extraction differences, format-induced parsing success, and additional decoding compute, and vanish against matched-format matched-compute baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparing chain-of-thought against controlled baselines that equalize output format, answer extraction, and token budget will show gains shrinking toward zero on a majority of visual reasoning benchmarks tested.
why_important: If the technique's visual gains are evaluation artifacts, product and research effort premised on multimodal reasoning-by-verbalization is misdirected.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Format-confound critiques exist for language benchmarks; a rigorous controlled null test specifically for visual reasoning tasks may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate open multimodal models on several visual reasoning benchmarks under chain-of-thought and matched-control prompting, with identical extraction pipelines and token budgets.
main_risk: Effects may be model-dependent, so the null must be tested across several model families before generalizing.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Verbalized step-by-step reasoning is assumed to improve visual problem solving.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The visual computation happens in the encoder and projection layers, and appending verbal steps may only change the output interface, not the perception.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One open model, one benchmark, chain-of-thought versus format-matched control; an evening of inference.

one_line_idea: Knowledge distillation from large vision foundation models transfers little beyond what label smoothing and better targets provide: a dark-knowledge null at foundation scale.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Distillation from large teachers is standard practice and its benefit is usually attributed to rich inter-class structure in teacher outputs.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] At foundation scale, matched baselines using smoothed or re-labeled targets without any teacher logits capture most of distillation's student improvement, implying the teacher's specific output structure contributes marginally.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Students trained with teacher logits versus with label-smoothing and teacher-free re-labeled targets at matched budgets will differ by much less than the gap usually attributed to distillation.
why_important: Distillation pipelines carry heavy engineering cost premised on dark knowledge; a null would simplify small-model production substantially.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Label-smoothing-versus-distillation comparisons exist for older setups; a decisive matched-budget decomposition with modern foundation teachers may be unresolved.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched students under teacher-logit distillation, label smoothing, and teacher-argmax relabeling on one dataset, and compare downstream accuracy and robustness.
main_risk: Distillation variants differ widely, and defenders can always cite an untested variant, so the study must cover the mainstream recipes.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Teacher output distributions are believed to carry substantial transferable dark knowledge.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Much of the measured benefit may come from target noise reduction and regularization, which cheaper mechanisms replicate.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One student architecture, three target types, one dataset; three training runs of moderate cost.

one_line_idea: Adversarial robustness gains do not transfer across threat models: a systematic cross-threat evaluation matrix showing mostly empty off-diagonals for modern vision defenses.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Defenses are typically evaluated within the threat model they were trained for, and cross-threat results are reported sparsely and inconsistently.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For current defended vision models, robustness earned under one perturbation family provides little protection under other families and under realistic non-norm-bounded attacks, so single-threat robustness numbers systematically overstate practical security.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A full defense-by-attack evaluation matrix across perturbation families will show off-diagonal robustness collapsing toward undefended baselines for most defense-attack pairs.
why_important: Security claims consumed by deployers implicitly promise general robustness; an empty off-diagonal matrix quantifies how misleading that promise is.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Cross-threat brittleness has been noted for older defenses; a maintained comprehensive matrix covering current foundation-scale defended models may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble public defended checkpoints, run a standardized attack battery spanning several perturbation families, and publish the full matrix with confidence intervals.
main_risk: Attack implementation quality determines the result's credibility, demanding strong adaptive attacks per cell.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A model robust under the standard threat model is casually described and consumed as robust.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Training against one perturbation family shapes decision boundaries only along that family's directions, leaving all other directions as undefended as before.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One defended checkpoint, two off-threat attacks, compare against its in-threat robustness; a day.

one_line_idea: Feature-space augmentation and mixing methods that helped small-scale training deliver no measurable benefit when fine-tuning foundation backbones: a scale-dependent null.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Interpolation-based and feature-space augmentation techniques are established for from-scratch training and are often carried over to fine-tuning workflows by default.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The regularization these methods provided is redundant with the implicit regularization of large-scale pretraining, so at fine-tuning time they add nothing or slightly hurt, and their continued use is cargo cult.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A multi-seed factorial study of fine-tuning with and without these augmentations across tasks and backbones will show effects statistically indistinguishable from zero for most cells.
why_important: Default recipes propagate through the field; documenting which components became inert avoids wasted complexity and misattributed gains.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual negative anecdotes circulate; a well-powered multi-seed null study covering the popular augmentation family at fine-tuning time may be unpublished because nulls are undervalued.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune three backbones on four tasks with and without each augmentation, ten seeds per cell, and report effect estimates with intervals.
main_risk: A null across tested cells cannot exclude benefits in untested regimes such as extreme low-data fine-tuning, so scope must be explicit.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Established augmentation techniques are assumed to remain beneficial in fine-tuning pipelines.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The data-hunger these methods addressed is precisely what pretraining removed.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One backbone, one task, augmentation on versus off, five seeds each; overlap check within days.

one_line_idea: Synthetic training images from generative models improve downstream benchmarks mainly when the test set shares the generator's stylistic biases, and gains evaporate on independently sourced test data.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Augmenting training with generative-model images is reported to help on standard benchmarks, and the practice is spreading.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Part of the reported gain arises because generator outputs and popular test sets share web-derived stylistic statistics, so synthetic data teaches test-set style rather than task content, and gains shrink on freshly captured test data.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Models trained with synthetic augmentation will show larger improvements on web-derived test sets than on matched freshly captured test sets of the same categories, with the difference statistically robust.
why_important: Synthetic data pipelines are being industrialized; if gains are style leakage, deployed models will disappoint outside benchmark-like inputs.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Synthetic-data papers report benchmark gains; a controlled web-versus-fresh test decomposition isolating style leakage may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with and without synthetic augmentation, evaluate on a web-derived test set and a freshly captured same-category test set, and compare gain sizes.
main_risk: Fresh capture introduces its own distribution differences beyond style, requiring careful category and context matching.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Synthetic augmentation gains are read as genuine task-level improvements.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The generator was trained on the same web distribution as the benchmarks, making style-matching the path of least resistance for measured gains.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Use an existing fresh-capture dataset for shared categories, evaluate public synthetic-augmented versus baseline checkpoints where available; days.

one_line_idea: Human-level performance claims in vision rest on weak human baselines, and expert or incentive-aligned human evaluation reopens the human-machine gap on several solved tasks.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Human baselines on vision benchmarks are typically collected from crowdworkers under time and pay conditions that discourage careful work, and these numbers anchor human-level claims.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Human accuracy measured with domain-familiar annotators, adequate time, training on the label taxonomy, and accuracy-based incentives is substantially higher than the cited baselines, reversing some claimed machine-over-human results.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-measuring human performance on tasks with prominent human-level claims under strengthened protocols will produce baselines above current model scores in at least some cases.
why_important: Human-level claims shape policy, hiring of automation, and research priorities; if the reference point is an artifact of cheap annotation, the claims mislead broadly.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual strengthened-baseline studies exist for specific benchmarks; a systematic protocol-sensitivity study of human baselines across prominent claims may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select three tasks with cited human-level claims, re-collect human baselines under weak and strengthened protocols, and compare protocol effects to human-machine gaps.
main_risk: Strengthened protocols are expensive and their design choices will be contested, requiring pre-registration.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Cited human baselines are treated as reasonable estimates of human capability on the task.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The baseline measures the economics of crowdsourcing, not the psychophysics of human vision.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One task, twenty careful incentivized annotators on a few hundred items versus the cited baseline; a week including recruitment.

one_line_idea: Models beating human accuracy on benchmarks are often just out-predicting annotator disagreement: agreement-ceiling analysis reframes superhuman claims as majority-vote overfitting.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmark ground truth is usually a majority vote over annotators whose disagreement rate is nonzero, and model accuracy is computed against that vote.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Where models exceed measured human accuracy, a substantial share of the excess comes from predicting the majority-vote artifact on ambiguous items rather than superior perception, and evaluation against full annotator label distributions removes much of the superhuman margin.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Scoring models against annotator distributions rather than hard majority labels will shrink model-over-human margins on ambiguous item strata while leaving unambiguous strata unchanged.
why_important: Superhuman claims imply models can replace human judgment; if the margin lives on ambiguous items where ground truth is a coin-flip convention, the implication fails.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Soft-label evaluation exists as a technique; using it to systematically deconstruct superhuman vision claims may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Obtain or collect per-item annotator distributions for one benchmark with superhuman claims, stratify by agreement level, and compare model-human margins per stratum under hard and soft scoring.
main_risk: Per-annotator data is unavailable for many benchmarks and expensive to recreate.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Exceeding the human baseline on a benchmark is interpreted as exceeding human perceptual ability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: On items where humans genuinely disagree, matching the majority vote measures conformity to an aggregation rule, not visual competence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Use any benchmark with released per-annotator labels, stratify by agreement, and recompute one model's margin; hours.

one_line_idea: Ground truth is instruction-dependent: re-annotating the same images under different but equally reasonable instructions shifts model rankings, exposing benchmark truth as one convention among several.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Annotation instructions make choices about edge cases, granularity, and precedence that could reasonably be made differently, and models are ranked against one instruction realization.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model rankings are not invariant to defensible instruction variants, because different models align differently with specific annotation conventions, so leaderboard order partially encodes arbitrary instruction decisions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-annotating a benchmark sample under three defensible instruction variants and re-scoring a model pool will show ranking changes across variants exceeding annotation-noise controls.
why_important: If truth conventions drive rankings, benchmark authority over model comparison is weaker than assumed, and instruction publication plus multi-convention scoring becomes necessary.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Instruction effects on label quality are studied in annotation research; connecting instruction variation causally to model-ranking instability may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Design three instruction variants with experts, re-annotate one thousand items under each with matched annotator pools, and measure ranking stability of several checkpoints.
main_risk: Instruction variants must be defensibly equivalent in reasonableness, which needs external expert validation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Benchmark labels are treated as the truth about the images rather than one instruction-conditioned encoding of it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Every annotation project resolves ambiguity by fiat, and models trained on different data inherit different fiats.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two instruction variants, two hundred items, one annotator pool per variant, re-score three models; days.

one_line_idea: Evaluating against annotator label distributions instead of hard labels reranks vision foundation models, revealing that some models are better at truth and others at convention.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard evaluation collapses annotator judgments to a single hard label per item, discarding the disagreement structure.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model rankings under distribution-matching metrics, such as divergence from annotator label distributions, differ materially from hard-label accuracy rankings, and the difference identifies models that capture human perceptual uncertainty versus models that exploit aggregation conventions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On benchmarks with per-annotator data, ranking by distributional divergence will disagree with accuracy ranking for a nontrivial fraction of model pairs, concentrated among top performers.
why_important: Applications differ in whether they need conventional answers or honest ambiguity representation; a single hard metric hides which model suits which need.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Soft-label scoring exists; a systematic reranking study across modern foundation checkpoints with an interpretation framework for the disagreements may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect model predictive distributions on benchmarks with per-annotator labels, compute both metric families, and analyze pairwise rank disagreement.
main_risk: Annotator distributions confound perceptual ambiguity with annotator population idiosyncrasy, requiring demographic robustness checks.
community_default_belief: [KNOWN FACT] Hard-label accuracy is the default and usually sole reported comparison metric.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Collapsing a distribution to its mode before scoring destroys exactly the information that distinguishes calibrated perception from convention-fitting.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark with released annotator distributions, five models, two metrics; hours with cached predictions.

one_line_idea: Model-assisted annotation has quietly contaminated ground truth: benchmarks labeled with model-in-the-loop pipelines are biased toward the model families used, inflating those families' measured performance.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Modern datasets increasingly use model proposals, pre-labeling, or verification assistance during annotation to cut cost, and the assisting models come from a small set of families.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Annotator anchoring on model proposals imprints the assisting model's error patterns and category conventions into the labels, so related models score higher on such benchmarks for reasons unrelated to capability, creating a self-preference loop at the dataset level.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparing model rankings on assisted-labeled versus independently-labeled subsets of the same data will show a measurable advantage for models related to the assisting family, absent in the independent subset.
why_important: As assisted annotation becomes universal, benchmarks stop being independent measurements and start echoing incumbent model behavior, entrenching leaders.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Anchoring bias in annotation is documented in human-computer interaction research; tracing it through to benchmark-level model-ranking distortion may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate one image set twice, with and without model assistance from a known family, then evaluate related and unrelated models against both label sets and compare relative scores.
main_risk: Assisted and unassisted annotation differ in error rates too, so the analysis must separate bias direction from label quality.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Assisted annotation is treated as a cost optimization that leaves label validity unchanged.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Human reviewers accept plausible proposals at high rates, so the proposal distribution becomes the label distribution wherever attention lapses.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Five hundred images annotated both ways with one assisting model, evaluate two related and two unrelated checkpoints; days including annotation.

one_line_idea: Quality-control gold questions bias test sets toward the unambiguous, so benchmarks systematically exclude the hard cases and overstate deployable accuracy.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Crowdsourcing pipelines filter annotators and items using agreement thresholds and gold questions, discarding items where annotators disagree.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The discarded high-disagreement items are not noise but a coherent hard stratum of the task distribution, and model accuracy on that stratum is far below benchmark scores, meaning quality control mechanically inflates reported capability.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Recovering and expert-adjudicating items dropped by agreement filters for one benchmark will yield a stratum where model accuracy is dramatically lower, and the stratum's size will imply a material downward correction to effective task accuracy.
why_important: Deployment inputs include the ambiguous cases benchmarks filtered out, so the filtering constitutes a structural optimism bias in all downstream expectations.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Annotation filtering is standard practice discussed as quality assurance; quantifying its selection effect on measured model capability may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Obtain or reconstruct the pre-filter item pool for one dataset, expert-adjudicate a dropped-item sample, evaluate models on it, and compare against the published test set.
main_risk: Pre-filter pools are rarely archived, possibly forcing a prospective study with a newly collected dataset.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Agreement filtering is assumed to remove annotation noise while leaving the task distribution representative.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Disagreement correlates with genuine input difficulty, so filtering on it truncates the difficulty distribution itself.
fastest_falsification_experiment: In any dataset releasing agreement scores, compare model accuracy on high-versus-low agreement items; hours if metadata exists.

one_line_idea: Vision-language models used as judges of visual outputs exhibit self-preference and family-preference biases large enough to corrupt model comparisons that rely on them.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Model-as-judge protocols are spreading from text evaluation into visual tasks such as captioning, editing quality, and grounded dialogue, because human evaluation is expensive.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Multimodal judges systematically favor outputs from themselves and from models sharing their training lineage, with bias magnitude comparable to the quality differences being measured, so judge-based visual leaderboards are structurally distorted.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A round-robin experiment where multiple multimodal judges score identity-masked outputs from multiple generators will show statistically significant judge-generator interaction effects aligned with model lineage.
why_important: Judge-based evaluation is becoming the field's scalability answer; unquantified lineage bias would silently rig comparisons across the ecosystem.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Self-preference is documented for text judges; a rigorous lineage-bias quantification for visual judging tasks may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Cross several judges with several generators on caption and edit-quality tasks, mask identities, include human-rated anchors, and estimate interaction effects.
main_risk: Output style may correlate with lineage for legitimate quality reasons, requiring human anchors to separate bias from true quality.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A strong multimodal judge is assumed to be an approximately neutral scorer of other models' visual outputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Judges score outputs partly by their likelihood under the judge's own distribution, which is exactly what lineage relatives maximize.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two judges, three generators, five hundred masked comparisons with a small human anchor set; days.

one_line_idea: Annotation-vendor ecosystems create test-set leakage paths that deduplication cannot see: the same worker pools and internal guideline documents touch both training-data production and benchmark creation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A small number of annotation vendors and worker platforms service both dataset construction for model training and benchmark annotation, with shared workforces, tooling, and convention documents.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Convention leakage through shared annotation ecosystems aligns training labels with benchmark labels at the level of edge-case handling, giving models trained on vendor-labeled data an unearned benchmark advantage invisible to image-level contamination audits.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Models trained on data labeled under one vendor's conventions will show a measurable edge-case-item advantage on benchmarks annotated under the same conventions, relative to convention-mismatched benchmarks with matched difficulty.
why_important: This is a contamination channel operating on labels rather than images, currently outside every audit framework, and it advantages incumbents with vendor relationships.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Contamination research focuses on data overlap; a convention-leakage framing with an empirical edge-case methodology may be entirely new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Identify benchmark and training datasets with documented shared versus distinct annotation origins, construct edge-case item sets, and test for convention-aligned accuracy advantages.
main_risk: Annotation provenance is poorly documented, making origin classification the weakest link of the study.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Benchmarks annotated independently of a model's training data are assumed to be uncontaminated tests of it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Labels encode conventions, conventions travel through people and documents, and the industry concentrates both in a few organizations.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare model rankings on edge-case items across two benchmarks of the same task known to use different annotation vendors; days once item sets are built.

one_line_idea: A field-wide bootstrap audit of vision benchmark deltas: a large fraction of published improvements are within test-set resampling noise once paired item-level uncertainty is computed.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision papers overwhelmingly report point-estimate benchmark scores without confidence intervals or paired significance tests, while claimed margins have shrunk over time.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Applying paired item-level bootstrap to a broad sample of published improvement claims will show that a substantial fraction do not exceed resampling noise, and the non-significant fraction has grown over publication years as margins shrank.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Reproducing a systematically sampled set of claimed improvements and computing paired intervals will find a material share of claims whose intervals cover zero, with the share increasing in recent years.
why_important: The field's self-narrative of steady progress depends on trusting small deltas; quantifying their statistical emptiness recalibrates literature-reading and reviewing norms.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Significance critiques exist in adjacent fields; a large-scale executed audit over vision benchmark claims with temporal analysis may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample fifty claimed improvements with reproducible checkpoints, evaluate both models per claim on the original test sets, and compute paired bootstrap intervals per claim.
