one_line_idea: Reported multimodal reasoning gains on text-rich benchmarks are mostly optical-character-recognition gains in disguise, separable by transcribed-input ablations.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmarks involving documents, charts, and text-in-image are scored end-to-end, so recognition quality and reasoning quality contribute inseparably to the reported number.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Cross-model differences on text-rich visual benchmarks are dominated by recognition quality, and providing ground-truth transcriptions equalizes models far more than reasoning-difference narratives predict.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating models with and without oracle transcriptions will show large gap compression under oracle input, attributing most of the original gaps to recognition rather than reasoning.
why_important: Model cards and marketing attribute text-rich benchmark leads to reasoning; misattribution distorts both buyer decisions and research investment.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Component ablations exist in document-understanding research; a systematic recognition-versus-reasoning decomposition across current multimodal models may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select text-rich benchmarks with recoverable transcriptions, evaluate a model pool with raw images versus oracle-text-plus-image input, and decompose the gaps.
main_risk: Oracle transcription changes the task interface and could disadvantage models tuned for pixel-space text reading.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Leads on text-rich visual benchmarks are read as multimodal reasoning superiority.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The bottleneck component determines the score, and recognition is plausibly the bottleneck for most current systems.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, two models with a known gap, oracle-transcription ablation; a day.

one_line_idea: Chart and diagram question-answering benchmarks are contaminated by template reuse: finite generator templates make test items predictable from training exposure, inflating scores.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Many chart-understanding benchmarks are produced by programmatic generators or curated from web sources with recurring chart-library styles and question templates.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models exploit template regularities in axes, palettes, and question phrasing, so performance on template-novel charts drops sharply, and benchmark scores overstate chart-reading capability by the template-familiarity margin.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating models on style-transferred or newly-templated charts encoding identical data will show substantial accuracy drops relative to standard test items, with drop size correlated with the benchmark's template concentration.
why_important: Chart understanding is a headline enterprise capability; template-inflated scores misrepresent readiness for real heterogeneous documents.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Template concerns are mentioned anecdotally; a controlled same-data different-template evaluation across current models may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-render a benchmark subset's underlying data with novel templates, verify answer preservation, and compare model accuracy on original versus re-rendered items.
main_risk: Re-rendering may inadvertently change legibility, requiring human verification that items remain fairly answerable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Chart benchmark accuracy is treated as general chart-comprehension ability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Generators sample from small template spaces, and web-scale pretraining has seen those spaces exhaustively.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Twenty benchmark charts re-rendered in one unusual style, answered by two models; drop measurement in a day.

one_line_idea: Multi-image reasoning benchmarks are largely answerable from a single image, and single-image ablations expose that the multi-image capability being marketed is untested by them.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] New benchmarks claim to test reasoning across multiple images, and models are marketed on multi-image capabilities certified by those scores.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Due to construction shortcuts, a large fraction of multi-image items are solvable from the single most informative image, so benchmark scores mostly measure single-image understanding plus image selection, not cross-image integration.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating models given only the best single image per item will recover a large fraction of full multi-image performance, and the recoverable fraction will vary enough across benchmarks to rerank their validity.
why_important: Cross-image integration is a distinct capability needed for real workflows such as comparison shopping and medical series reading; unvalidated benchmarks certify it falsely.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Ablation-based validity audits exist for video benchmarks; applying the single-image ablation systematically to the new generation of multi-image benchmarks may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For each benchmark item, evaluate models under all single-image ablations, record maximum single-image performance, and report the multi-image necessity fraction per benchmark.
main_risk: Image-selection itself uses some cross-image processing, blurring the ablation's interpretation unless selection is oracle-provided.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Multi-image benchmark scores are read as evidence of cross-image reasoning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Writing questions that genuinely require integrating disjoint visual evidence is hard, and benchmark construction pipelines default to easier item types.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, one model, oracle-best-single-image ablation on a few hundred items; an evening.

one_line_idea: Video-understanding benchmarks remain largely solvable from one or a few frames even for the newest foundation models, so temporal-understanding claims are still uncertified.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Single-frame solvability was demonstrated for older video benchmarks, and new benchmarks plus new models have since appeared with renewed temporal-understanding claims.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The single-frame shortcut persists in the current benchmark generation because item construction economics did not change, so current temporal-capability claims rest on benchmarks that still do not require time.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Frame-ablated and frame-shuffled evaluations of current models on current video benchmarks will recover most of the full-video scores, with genuinely temporal items forming a small identifiable minority.
why_important: Video capability drives major compute investments and product claims; certifying it with time-indifferent benchmarks misleads the entire stack.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The critique is established for older benchmarks; the contrarian contribution is demonstrating its persistence in the newest benchmark generation and providing a certified temporal-item subset, which may be undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run single-frame, sparse-frame, and shuffled-frame ablations for several current models on the newest video benchmarks, and publish per-benchmark temporal-necessity scores.
main_risk: Some models degrade under frame ablation for interface rather than capability reasons, requiring input-format controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] New video benchmarks are assumed to have fixed the single-frame solvability problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The incentive to produce many items cheaply still favors questions answerable from appearances rather than dynamics.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One new benchmark, one model, middle-frame-only evaluation; recovery fraction by tomorrow.

one_line_idea: Counting benchmarks are gamed by dataset count priors: models predict the modal count for an object category rather than counting, and prior-decorrelated items collapse performance.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Counting evaluation items are drawn from natural image distributions where object counts per category follow predictable skewed distributions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Much of measured counting ability is category-conditional count-prior regression, and evaluation on items where true counts deviate from category modes will show performance collapsing toward prior-predictable levels.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Stratifying counting benchmarks by deviation from category modal counts will show steep accuracy decay with deviation, and a prior-only baseline will match models on low-deviation strata.
why_important: Counting is presented as a milestone of visual precision; prior-driven scores misstate whether models can actually enumerate.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Count-prior concerns appear in visual question answering history; a deviation-stratified audit of current foundation models with prior baselines may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute category count distributions from benchmark metadata, build deviation strata, evaluate models and a prior-only baseline per stratum.
main_risk: High-deviation natural images may be visually atypical in other ways, confounding deviation with general difficulty.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Counting benchmark accuracy is read as enumeration capability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Predicting the mode of a skewed distribution scores well without any counting, and benchmarks sampled from nature reward exactly that.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, accuracy on modal-count items versus off-modal items for one model; hours with existing annotations.

one_line_idea: Safety evaluations of multimodal models measure refusal-style pattern matching rather than harm-relevant capability, and style-normalized re-evaluation reorders safety leaderboards.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multimodal safety benchmarks score whether models refuse or comply on curated prompt sets, with grading often keyed to refusal phrasing.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Safety scores are dominated by superficial refusal-style alignment with graders, so models can score safely while remaining capable of harm under rephrased elicitation, and style-normalized adversarial evaluation will substantially reorder safety rankings.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Applying systematic elicitation variations and grading on outcome rather than style will show large per-model score movements and ranking changes relative to standard safety benchmark results.
why_important: Safety leaderboards inform deployment gates and public trust; if they measure etiquette rather than safety, the gates are decorative.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Jailbreak research shows brittleness; converting that insight into a validity critique with style-normalized safety scoring for multimodal models may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-evaluate models on one safety benchmark under elicitation-varied prompts with outcome-based human grading, and compare rankings with the standard protocol.
main_risk: Outcome-based grading of unsafe content requires careful ethics protocols and restricted handling.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Higher refusal-benchmark scores are taken to mean safer models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Refusal is a surface behavior trained separately from capability, and graders keyed to surface forms measure the training of the surface.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Twenty benchmark items, five elicitation variants each, one model, outcome-graded; days under proper safety protocols.

one_line_idea: Instruction-following evaluations for multimodal models conflate formatting compliance with visual understanding: parsing-tolerant re-grading changes model rankings.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Automated multimodal evaluations extract answers via format-sensitive parsers, and models differ in how reliably they emit the expected formats.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A measurable share of cross-model score differences on instruction-following visual benchmarks comes from parser compatibility rather than task competence, and semantic re-grading with robust extraction reorders models.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-grading raw model outputs with human or robust-semantic extraction will recover credit for format-noncompliant correct answers non-uniformly across models, changing several rankings.
why_important: Leaderboard positions shift products and research priorities; crediting parser luck as capability corrupts those signals at near-zero visibility.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Extraction-error concerns circulate among practitioners; a quantified parser-attributable variance analysis across multimodal leaderboards may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample items across models from one leaderboard's raw outputs, dual-grade with strict parsing and semantic grading, and estimate parser-attributable score components.
main_risk: Semantic grading introduces judge subjectivity, requiring inter-grader reliability reporting.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Automated benchmark scores are treated as measuring the intended visual capability rather than output formatting.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The parser is a hidden second task, and models were unevenly trained for it.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two hundred failed items from one model on one benchmark, manually re-graded for semantic correctness; the recovered fraction is the effect size, in one day.

one_line_idea: Temporal collection order inside benchmarks violates the iid assumption invisibly: items collected later differ systematically, and train-test splits inherit hidden temporal structure.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmark items are collected over weeks or years of scraping and annotation, and split protocols ignore collection timestamps entirely.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Collection-time metadata predicts item properties such as source mix, category balance, and annotation conventions, so random splits contain exploitable temporal structure and time-respecting splits yield lower, more honest generalization estimates.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A classifier will predict items' collection periods above chance from content alone, and models evaluated on time-respecting splits will score measurably below random-split evaluation on the same data.
why_important: The iid split is the silent axiom under every benchmark number; measuring its violation quantifies a bias affecting the entire evaluation edifice.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temporal splits are standard in some applied domains; auditing mainstream vision benchmarks for internal temporal structure may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Recover collection timestamps for one benchmark, train period-prediction probes, and compare model scores under random versus time-respecting splits.
main_risk: Timestamps are unavailable for many datasets, restricting the audit to benchmarks with recoverable provenance.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Benchmark items are treated as exchangeable samples from a fixed distribution.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Data collection is a temporal process with drifting sources and conventions, and randomizing indices does not erase what the process baked in.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one dataset with timestamps, train a quick probe to predict collection year from the image; above-chance accuracy in hours falsifies exchangeability.

one_line_idea: Benchmark category weighting reflects collection accidents rather than deployment frequency, and usage-weighted evaluation changes which vision models look best.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmark class and task compositions were determined by what was collectible, and evaluation weights all items equally within that accidental composition.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Weighting evaluation by empirical usage frequencies from real application logs, rather than by benchmark composition, changes model rankings, because models differ on categories whose benchmark weight mismatches deployment weight most.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-weighting existing per-item results under several empirically-derived usage profiles will produce ranking changes relative to uniform weighting, exceeding bootstrap noise.
why_important: Evaluation exists to predict deployment value, and composition-accident weighting breaks that link at the aggregation step regardless of item quality.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Importance weighting is standard statistics; grounding vision-benchmark weights in measured application usage distributions may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Derive category usage profiles from public application telemetry or search statistics, re-weight cached benchmark results for a model pool, and quantify ranking sensitivity.
main_risk: Usage profiles vary across applications, so results must be presented per profile rather than as a new universal ranking.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Uniform item weighting is assumed to be the neutral default for aggregate scores.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Uniformity over an arbitrary composition is not neutrality; it is an unexamined weighting choice inherited from collection logistics.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Reweight cached per-class results for five models under one plausible usage profile; an hour of analysis.

one_line_idea: The single-ground-truth assumption fails on a measurable fraction of benchmark images, and ambiguity-aware evaluation that accepts answer sets changes both scores and rankings.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Evaluation frameworks assume each item has exactly one correct answer, while images routinely admit multiple defensible interpretations due to occlusion, granularity choices, and polysemous categories.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Enumerating defensible answer sets for benchmark items and scoring against sets rather than single labels will materially change absolute scores and some model orderings, and the ambiguous fraction is large enough to matter at current frontier margins.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Expert enumeration of defensible answers for a benchmark sample will find multi-answer items at a rate comparable to frontier model gaps, and set-based re-scoring will shift rankings for model pairs whose differences concentrate on ambiguous items.
why_important: At today's accuracy levels, the ambiguous stratum is the battleground stratum, and scoring it against arbitrary single labels randomizes frontier comparisons.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multi-label re-annotation exists for specific datasets; a general ambiguity-aware scoring framework with quantified ranking impact across benchmarks may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Expert-annotate defensible answer sets for one thousand items on one benchmark, re-score a model pool set-wise, and compare with standard scoring.
main_risk: Deciding defensibility is itself a judgment call, requiring documented criteria and multiple experts.
community_default_belief: [KNOWN FACT] Standard evaluation treats one stored label per item as the complete truth.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The world under-determines single answers for many images, and forcing uniqueness converts genuine ties into arbitrary wins and losses.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two experts enumerate answers for two hundred items; the multi-answer rate versus the frontier gap is the headline number, within days.

one_line_idea: The assumption that higher pretraining data quality uniformly improves downstream performance is wrong: quality filtering helps some downstream tasks while measurably hurting others, and the trade-off is hidden by suite averages.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Data-quality filtering is applied globally during pretraining under the assumption that cleaner data is better for downstream performance in general.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Quality filters remove data strata, such as low-quality imagery, unusual viewpoints, and degraded captures, that specific downstream tasks depend on, so per-task analysis will reveal reproducible harms from filtering that aggregate reporting conceals.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Pretraining matched models on filtered versus unfiltered pools and evaluating on a broad task battery will show a subset of tasks, plausibly those involving degraded or atypical imagery, where the unfiltered model wins consistently.
why_important: Filtering decisions are made once and inherited by every downstream user; unmeasured per-task harms mean some application communities are silently paying for others' gains.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Data-quality research reports aggregate gains; a harm-focused per-task decomposition of filtering effects may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain paired mid-scale models on filtered and unfiltered versions of one pool, evaluate on a task battery including degraded-input tasks, and test for reproducible per-task reversals.
main_risk: Mid-scale results may not extrapolate, and the harmed-task set could differ at production scale.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Data-quality filtering is assumed beneficial or neutral for essentially all downstream uses.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Quality is defined relative to a curator's aesthetic, and tasks that live in the discarded stratum lose their training signal by definition.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate existing public checkpoints known to differ mainly in filtering strictness on two degraded-input tasks; a day if such checkpoint pairs exist.

one_line_idea: English-centric class names and prompts are an ignored evaluation assumption: multilingual re-evaluation of zero-shot vision models changes rankings and reveals language-dependent capability profiles.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Zero-shot vision evaluation almost universally uses English class names and prompts, while models differ in multilingual pretraining exposure.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model rankings under non-English class vocabularies differ substantially from English rankings, and English evaluation systematically overstates the relative quality of English-dominant models for the majority-world deployment contexts where other languages define the labels.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating a model pool with translated and localized class vocabularies across several languages will show reproducible ranking changes and per-model language sensitivity profiles diverging from the English-based leaderboard.
why_important: Global deployments interface with local vocabularies; an English-only evaluation convention misestimates model value for most of the world's users.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multilingual vision-language work exists; framing English evaluation as a ranking-distorting assumption with a cross-language rank-stability audit may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build validated class-name translations for one benchmark in five languages, evaluate a model pool per language, and quantify ranking stability across languages.
main_risk: Translation quality and cultural category mismatches must be controlled, or effects could reflect bad translations rather than model properties.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] English-based zero-shot scores are treated as language-neutral measures of visual capability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The text encoder is half the zero-shot system, and its quality is sharply language-dependent in ways the convention never measures.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, two languages, three models; rank-stability check in a day with existing translation resources.

one_line_idea: Static test sets cannot detect interaction brittleness: adaptive human-in-the-loop evaluation finds failure modes in vision foundation models that static benchmarks structurally miss, at measurable rates.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Evaluation practice is overwhelmingly static, scoring fixed item sets, while deployed multimodal systems face adaptive users who probe, rephrase, and follow up.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Adaptive adversarial evaluation, where trained humans interactively search for failures within a fixed query budget, will uncover consistent failure modes invisible to static benchmarks, and models with equal static scores will separate widely under adaptive testing.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Under a standardized adaptive protocol with fixed interaction budgets, evaluators will find reproducible failures at rates uncorrelated with static benchmark scores across a model pool, demonstrating that static scores do not order interactive reliability.
why_important: Users experience models interactively, so an evaluation paradigm blind to interaction measures something other than the deployed experience.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Red-teaming exists as practice; formalizing budgeted adaptive evaluation as a reproducible metric with static-score comparison for vision models may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define an adaptive evaluation protocol with budget and reproducibility rules, run trained evaluators against several models with matched static scores, and compare failure-discovery rates.
main_risk: Evaluator skill variance threatens reproducibility, requiring evaluator normalization and inter-evaluator agreement measurement.
community_default_belief: [KNOWN FACT] Static benchmark scores are the standard and usually only certification of vision model quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Static sets sample the input space independently of the model, while real failure discovery is a search process that exploits model-specific weaknesses.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two models with matched static scores, two evaluators, fixed one-hour budgets per model; compare discovered-failure counts within a week.
